issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was forty-eight when the warehouse fire took everything. He had been working as a substance abuse counselor for nearly two decades, a job he loved—one that gave him purpose, that let him sit across from people at their worst and say, I understand, and mean it. The warehouse was being used as a temporary shelter for unhoused clients while renovations continued at the main facility. Marcus had volunteered to stay late that evening, helping a young woman named Keisha work through a relapse urge. The smell of the place was familiar: industrial cleaning solution, old concrete, the particular staleness of a space too many people had slept in. Around eleven, someone—they were never certain who—had left a space heater too close to a storage area packed with old mattresses and donated clothing.

The fire moved faster than anyone expected. Marcus was on the second floor when he heard the first alarm. He got Keisha out, then went back. He was certain there were people still inside, though afterward the investigators said the building had been cleared. He didn't remember much of the next minutes—the smoke so thick he couldn't see his own hands, the heat pressing down, a sound like nothing he'd ever heard before. He was pulled out by firefighters, barely conscious. Three people did die that night. Marcus was not one of them, but he had survived something he believed he should not have, and that knowledge never quite left him.

In the months that followed, Marcus noticed his body had become unreliable. A car backfiring would send his heart into a gallop. The smell of burnt toast in the break room at work would freeze him mid-sentence. He became hyperaware that his body was responding as if danger were still present, as if the warehouse were still burning around him. He had come to believe that this vigilance, this constant readiness, was the only thing keeping him safe—that if he let his guard down for even a moment, something catastrophic would happen. He could not afford to relax. The world was fundamentally unsafe, and only his exhausting, unceasing watchfulness stood between him and disaster.

When someone threw a pen across the room during a staff meeting—a frustrated gesture, nothing more—Marcus flinched so violently that everyone went quiet. After that, he began avoiding his colleagues. He stopped attending the weekly team lunches. He made excuses when friends called. The isolation seemed necessary; being around people meant being around unpredictability, and unpredictability meant danger. But the avoidance came with a cost. His supervisor asked if something was wrong. His best friend of fifteen years stopped reaching out. Marcus told himself this was acceptable, a small price for safety, though the loneliness accumulated like scar tissue.

The memories themselves had become strange and intrusive. Sometimes a burnt smell—a neighbor's barbecue, a restaurant kitchen—would trigger not just fear but a full sensory replay: he could smell the acrid smoke again, feel the heat on his face, taste ash. Other times, the emotional intensity of the event would flood through him without any image at all, a wave of terror and helplessness that seemed to come from nowhere, leaving him gasping and uncertain whether he was actually in danger. And most disturbing was the sense that these memories didn't quite belong to him. When he tried to think about what happened, it felt like he was remembering someone else's experience, watching himself from outside, which only deepened his fear that something fundamental had broken inside him.

He tried not to think about the fire. But trying not to think about it meant monitoring his own thoughts constantly, watching for any sign that he was thinking about it, which meant he was always, in a sense, thinking about it. He was terrified that if he allowed himself to really contemplate what had happened—the weight of it, the randomness, the lives lost—he would not be able to handle it. His mind would fracture. He would lose the thread entirely. So he pushed the thoughts away whenever they surfaced, but the pushing itself became exhausting, and the triggers kept pulling him back: the smell of smoke, the sight of someone throwing something, the simple fact of existing in a world where fires happened and people died and his own body could not be trusted to know the difference between then and now.

It was his supervisor who finally insisted. After Marcus made an error in a client session—losing his temper when a client raised his voice, something he would never have done before—she said he needed to talk to someone. Marcus resisted for weeks. He was the counselor, not the one who needed counseling. But the isolation was deepening, his sleep was fragmenting, and the constant monitoring of his own thoughts had become so consuming that he could barely focus on his clients. At fifty-five, Marcus came to his first appointment with a therapist, carrying the weight of seven years of hypervigilance, the loneliness of self-imposed exile, and a terror that the fire had fundamentally changed who he was—that the man he'd been before was someone else entirely, and that man was never coming back.
